claims.claim: The thesis is a 2023 Aalto University master's thesis (Mathematics and Operations Research, Complex Systems), i.e., a primary academic source, but not a peer-reviewed journal article; the exact correlation coefficients were not retrievable because the repository host (aaltodoc.aalto.fi) was unreachable during extraction and only abstract text from search snippets was available.
claims.quote: The thesis was authored by Liva Westerback and completed in 2023 as part of the Master's Programme in Mathematics and Operations Research in the Department of Complex Systems.

claims.claim: Traffic volume on a road segment can be modeled as a linear combination of two network centrality measures: closeness centrality (proxy for origin-destination trips) and betweenness centrality (proxy for pass-by trips), with road-type-weighted path-distance (PD = Ty*MD) used to compute the centralities.
claims.quote: The proposed method combines two network centrality measures abstracting the traffic volume on a road segment as the sum of origin-destination trips (i.e., Closeness-Centrality) and pass-by trips (i.e., Betweenness-Centrality).

claims.claim: The centrality-only linear model achieved R2 > 0.92 on validation data in all five cities (Colombo 0.935, Phnom Penh 0.942, Hanoi 0.923, Karachi 0.951, Dar es Salaam 0.959) with median absolute percentage error between 10.5% and 17.3%.
claims.quote: "R2: 0.935" (Colombo), "MdAPE: 17.15%" (Colombo); "R2: 0.942" (Phnom Penh), "MdAPE: 15.94%" (Phnom Penh); "R2: 0.923" (Hanoi), "MdAPE: 12.8%" (Hanoi); "R2: 0.951" (Karachi), "MdAPE: 10.5%" (Karachi); "R2: 0.959" (Dares Salaam), "MdAPE: 17.3%"

claims.claim: Betweenness centrality alone explains roughly 60% of the variability in segment traffic volume, while closeness centrality alone explains 32-35%; betweenness is the dominant exposure proxy.
claims.quote: BC can capture about 60% of the total variability ... CC also solely captures the 32%–35% of the variability

claims.claim: Centrality must be computed on a road-type (hierarchy) weighted network: segment cost is path-distance equal to metric length multiplied by a speed factor Ty assigned by road class (expressway/artery/collector/local), rather than pure metric length.
claims.quote: PD =Ty*MD ... MD measures the length of the road segment in kilometer ... Ty values by road hierarchy

claims.claim: The model coefficients are city-specific and must be recalibrated when transferred to a new area, although the model structure (BC + CC) is retained; the model does not capture seasonal or daily peak variation.
claims.quote: When applying this model elsewhere, it is recommended to recalibrate the parameters, without modifying the model structure

claims.claim: Nighttime light extracted specifically along freeways (SNPP-VIIRS 2015 annual composite, highway-oriented extraction) correlates with provincial freeway traffic flow volume at Pearson r = 0.905 for coaches and r = 0.731 for trucks.
claims.quote: Pearson Correlation Coefficient of freeway nighttime light and freeway traffic flow volume for coach and truck are 0.905 and 0.731, respectively

claims.claim: Restricting NTL to the road corridor is substantially more informative about traffic volume than total (area-wide) NTL: the correlation of total nighttime light with freeway traffic flow is only r = 0.593 (coach) and r = 0.516 (truck), versus 0.905 and 0.731 for road-extracted NTL.
claims.quote: which are higher than between freeway traffic flow volume for coach and truck and total nighttime light (0.593 and 0.516, respectively)

claims.claim: The NTL-based Highway Nighttime Traffic Prosperity Index (HNTPI) is strongly collinear with socio-economic variables at the provincial level: Pearson r with GDP per capita 0.772, consumption per capita 0.895, and population 0.968, implying road-corridor NTL largely proxies population/economic activity rather than traffic independently of it.
claims.quote: The Pearson Correlation Coefficient of HNTPI and gross domestic product (GDP) per capita, consumption per capita, and population are 0.772, 0.895, and 0.968, respectively.

claims.claim: The NTL-traffic relationship was established using SNPP-VIIRS 2015 annual nighttime light data and validated only at the provincial aggregation level in China (not at segment or grid-cell level), so transfer of the correlation to cell-level crash models is unverified in this source.
claims.quote: a highway-oriented method was proposed to extract highway nighttime light data from 2015 annual nighttime light data of the Suomi National Polar-Orbiting Partnership Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite sensor (SNPP-VIIRS). Subsequently, Pearson correlation analysis was used to fit the relationship between freeway traffic flow volume and freeway nighttime light at the provincial level.

claims.claim: Nighttime light along roads is highly spatially heterogeneous and strongest for lower-class national general highways in developed coastal/urban regions (e.g., Shanghai national general highway nighttime prosperity 22.34%), so NTL as an exposure proxy varies in meaning by road class and urbanization.
claims.quote: The national general highway is the most prosperous highway at night and the national general highway nighttime prosperity of Shanghai reached 22.34%.

claims.claim: Using only six Baidu POI count variables (banks, commercial buildings, retail shops, medical services, educational institutions, bus stops counted within a 500 m buffer of each 200 m OSM road segment) as predictors, random forest regression of NKDE vehicle-pedestrian collision density achieved out-of-bag R2 (OOB score) of 0.70-0.84 on arterial, secondary trunk and branch roads in Changning District, Shanghai, but below 0.1 on expressways.
claims.quote: Regardless of the period, the OOB scores of models with POI variables only (named POI-only models hereafter) for vehicle–pedestrian collisions ranged from 0.70 to 0.84 on the arterial, secondary trunk, and branch roads. [...] except for expressways (with OOB scores lower than 0.1), where people are usually not allowed to walk and where few pedestrian collisions happened.

claims.claim: The same POI-only proxies explain vehicle-vehicle crash density well on mid-hierarchy roads (OOB ~0.70 arterial, ~0.80 secondary trunk) but poorly on branch roads (~0.52-0.54) and expressways (<0.1), i.e. POI-based activity proxies substitute for exposure only where trips are local; for long-distance (expressway) traffic they fail.
claims.quote: The OOB scores of models for the arterial and secondary trunk roads were around 0.70 and 0.80, respectively, while the scores for the branch road models were only slightly above 0.50. It should also be noted that, similar to vehicle–pedestrian crashes, the OOB scores of POI-only models for vehicle–vehicle collisions on expressways were quite small (below 0.1)

claims.claim: Adding a single NPP-VIIRS nighttime-light feature (pixel value nearest the segment reference point, ~500 m resolution, nanoWatts/cm2/sr, raw and unstandardized) on top of POI counts raised OOB R2 by +4% to +10% on arterial/secondary roads and +16% on branch roads for vehicle-vehicle crashes (e.g. arterial 0.70 -> 0.77, branch 0.52 -> 0.60), and by 0-6% for vehicle-pedestrian crashes, with NTL showing low collinearity to POI counts (VIF 1.30).
claims.quote: Vehicle–Vehicle | Arterial | POI | 0.70 | 0.69 | POI + NTL | 0.77 (+10%) | 0.75 (+10%) | Secondary trunk | POI | 0.80 | 0.79 | POI + NTL | 0.83 (+4%) | 0.82 (+4%) | Branch | POI | 0.52 | 0.54 | POI + NTL | 0.60 (+16%) | 0.62 (+16%) [...] The integration of NTL has more positive impacts on the mapping of vehicle collision risk than on pedestrian safety.

claims.claim: The study's feature encoding was raw counts of POIs within a 500 m buffer around each 200 m road segment plus the nearest NTL pixel value, with no log transform, no density normalization and no standardization, justified by the use of tree-based (random forest) models; collinearity among these counts stayed below VIF 5 (max VIF 4.02 for retail shops).
claims.quote: NoBus | Number of bus stops within 500 m of each segment | [...] The NTL value of each road segment was taken from the pixel value closest to the reference point. [...] There was no need to standardize the input variables in the process of model construction, depending on the characteristics of the decision tree branch. [...] The VIF values of the variables are all below 5, illustrating low collinearity among variables.

claims.claim: Normalizing crashes by road length (an exposure proxy available directly from OSM) reverses the apparent ranking of road types: branch roads carry 44.3% of network length and 54.4% of pedestrian collisions (most dangerous per km for pedestrians), while expressways carry 19.6% of length but only 0.7% of vehicle-vehicle crashes.
claims.quote: Expressway | 71,361.66 (19.6%) | 5 (0.2%) | 519 (0.7%) | Arterial road | 91,691.49 (25.1%) | 672 (27.1%) | 26,784 (38.4%) | Secondary trunk road | 40,343.97 (11.1%) | 456 (18.4%) | 11,268 (16.2%) | Branch road | 161,605.70 (44.3%) | 1351 (54.4%) | 31,098 (44.6%) [...] It can be observed that branch roads are the most dangerous for pedestrians, while vehicles have a higher risk of colliding on arterial roads, if the length of roads is taken into consideration.

claims.claim: At the census-block-group level in Lincoln, NE (2,171 motorized-to-non-motorized crashes, 2011–2020), non-motorized exposure ('active miles' from calibrated StreetLight LBS data) correlates more strongly with crash counts (r=0.76) than vehicle miles (r=0.58), poverty rate (r=0.29) or non-white share (r=0.13, p=0.09).
claims.quote: Table 5.3 Quantitative Analysis of Crash Analysis — Variable / Correlation / P-Value: Vehicle Miles 0.58 0.00; Active Miles 0.76 0.00; Non-White Population 0.13 0.09; Poverty 0.29 0.00

claims.claim: When LBS activity indices are calibrated against intersection counts, land-use/road proxies add little beyond the activity index for pedestrians and vehicles, but matter for bicycles: random-forest feature importance for the StL volume index is 0.660 (pedestrian) and 0.785 (vehicle) vs 0.379 (bicycle), with number of lanes consistently second (0.128 / 0.048 / 0.253) and road network density third for bicycles (0.165).
claims.quote: In the bicycle model, the most important variable for influencing prediction accuracy was the Average Daily Zone Traffic (StL Volume). ... Average Daily Zone Traffic (StL Volume) 0.379; Number of lanes 0.253; Total road network density 0.165 ... An interesting observation from this model and the two previous models is the placement of the Number of lanes variable consistently ranking the second most important.

claims.claim: Raw LBS indices are far weaker proxies for non-motorized than motorized volume: StreetLight vehicle index vs. counts R2≈0.90, pedestrian R2≈0.60, bicycle R2≈0.25; adding EPA-SLD census-block-group covariates (population, occupied housing units, zero-car household share, employment) in linear regression lifts adj-R2 to 0.91 / 0.78 / 0.37 for vehicle / pedestrian / bicycle.
claims.quote: StL vehicle volumes correlated highly (R2 ≈ 0.90) with aggregated CoL counts. However, StL pedestrian volumes have a weaker correlation (R2 ≈ 0.60) than vehicle volumes and StL bicycle volumes performed even worse in this setting (R2 ≈ 0.25). ... Table 4.1 ... Vehicle 0.91 2263; Pedestrian 0.78 3348; Bicycle 0.37 3559

claims.claim: In a spatial-lag model of area-level non-motorized crash rate (crashes / (active miles × vehicle miles), 187 CBGs, pseudo-R2=0.23), multimodal network density (facility miles per sq mi) is the strongest positive predictor (effect size +112% per SD, p=0.00), while employment entropy (-89%, p=0.00), employment density (-76%, p=0.00), weighted intersection density (-59%, p=0.06) and walkability index (-68%, p=0.07) are negatively associated; one-car household share and low-wage worker share are positive (~+79%, p=0.01).
claims.quote: Network density in terms of facility miles of multi-modal links per square mile was highly statistically significant and had the largest effect size estimate. ... The walkability index was negatively correlated with multiplicative crash rate, with a moderate effect size and statistical significance. ... Network density in terms of facility miles of multi-modal links per square mile 0.010 112.27 0.00 ... Pseudo-R2 0.23 ... Number of Observations 187

claims.claim: The sign and significance of area-level land-use/density features depend on which exposure normalization is used (crashes/(active×vehicle miles), crashes/(active/vehicle ratio), crashes/active miles): e.g. three-leg multimodal intersection density is positive and significant under ratio (effect +57%, p=0.00) and active-miles (+17%, p=0.005) rates, while auto-removed intersection density is negative under multiplicative (p=0.06) and active-miles (p=0.029) rates; the report also warns that aggregating segment volumes to block groups inflates area volume when only a few segments carry traffic, and recommends effect sizes standardized per 1 SD because raw density variables were rescaled by 10,000.
claims.quote: It was found that results differ depending upon the exposure measure used to normalize crash counts. ... block group data may indicate a high volume, even when only specific street segments within that block group contribute, and the majority of the area in that block group lacks streets ... the effect size measures a percent change in the dependent variable for a one-standard- deviation change in the explanatory variable. This standardization helps to demonstrate the effect each variable has on the dependent variable, regardless of scale.

claims.claim: Using population (or population density) as a surrogate for pedestrian exposure in zonal pedestrian-crash models yields biased coefficient estimates: effects of several risk factors differed substantially between population-based and activity-based exposure models in 209 Hong Kong neighborhoods.
claims.quote: Our results indicated substantial inconsistencies in the effects of several risk factors between the models of population and activity-based exposure measures. [...] The use of population or population density as a surrogate for pedestrian exposure when modeling the frequency of zonal pedestrian crashes is expected to produce biased estimations and invalid inferences.

claims.claim: Among four pedestrian exposure measures (population, walking trips, walking time, walking distance), the model using number of walking trips had the best goodness-of-fit in a Bayesian spatially varying coefficients model of pedestrian-motor vehicle crash counts.
claims.quote: To dissect the role of pedestrian exposure, the estimated coefficients of models with population, walking trips, walking time, and walking distance as the measure of pedestrian exposure were presented and compared. [...] The model using walking trips as the measure of pedestrian exposure had the best goodness-of-fit.

claims.claim: After controlling for vehicle volume and pedestrian activity, road density, intersection density, bus stop density, and number of parking lots are positively associated with zonal pedestrian-motor vehicle crash frequency, while share of motorways and median monthly income are negatively associated.
claims.quote: After adjusting for vehicle volume and pedestrian activity, road density, intersection density, bus stop density, and the number of parking lots were found to be positively associated with PMV crash frequency, whereas the percentage of motorways and median monthly income had negative associations with the risk of PMV crashes.

claims.claim: Spatial heterogeneity in covariate effects (spatially varying coefficients) is non-negligible when modeling crashes over contiguous zones; heterogeneity arises from spatially correlated effects, not only unstructured variability.
claims.quote: We also provided new insights that in addition to the unstructured variability, heterogeneity in the effects of explanatory variables on the frequency of PMV crashes could also arise from the spatially correlated effects. [...] Spatial heterogeneity should also not be negligible when modeling pedestrian crashes involving contiguous spatial units.

claims.claim: Pedestrian exposure at zone level can be derived from crowdsourced travel-diary data by extracting pedestrian trajectories and aggregating them to neighborhoods (209 units in Hong Kong).
claims.quote: Based on a crowdsourced dataset in Hong Kong, we first proposed a procedure to extract pedestrian trajectories from travel-diary survey data. We then aggregated these data to 209 neighborhoods and developed a Bayesian spatially varying coefficients model

publishDate: 2020-10-01 (epub); Accident Analysis & Prevention vol. 148, December 2020, art. 105777, doi:10.1016/j.aap.2020.105777

claims.claim: In a crash-level injury-severity model for Changsha (2017–2019), SHAP on a CatBoost model ranked distance to nearest metro station first, road network density (per 1 km grid) third, POI mix (Shannon index within 1,000 m) fourth and distance to nearest bus stop fifth among all predictors, and 5D built-environment variables accounted for roughly 75% of total SHAP value.
claims.quote: 5D variables accounted for approximately 75% of the total SHAP value, whereas the non-5D variables accounted for roughly 25%.

claims.claim: Built-environment (5D) features alone are weak predictors of injury severity given a crash: CatBoost with 5D-only features reached ROC-AUC 0.774, versus 0.924 with crash-context (non-5D) features and 0.941 with both combined.
claims.quote: 5D-only CatBoost ROC-AUC: 0.773834; Non-5D CatBoost ROC-AUC: 0.924083; Combined ROC-AUC: 0.941496 ... The combined 5D + non-5D feature group consistently outperformed the models using either the 5D or non-5D feature group alone

claims.claim: The exposure/accessibility proxies were encoded as: road network density = total road length divided by grid area on a 1 km × 1 km grid (resolution chosen to match the 1 km population raster); POI mix = Shannon diversity index of POI categories in a 1,000 m buffer; destination accessibility = raw counts of schools, hospitals, malls, tourist attractions within 1,000 m; transit access = continuous distance in km to nearest metro station and bus stop.
claims.quote: The 1 km × 1 km grid was selected primarily because the smallest available spatial resolution of the population density data used in this study was 1 km.

claims.claim: Effect directions: injury risk increases nonlinearly with distance from the nearest metro station, while higher POI functional mix and higher road network density are associated with lower injury risk (SHAP shifts from positive to negative).
claims.quote: crash locations farther from metro stations exerted a stronger positive effect on traffic injury risk ... As POI mix increased from lower to higher levels, the SHAP value gradually shifted from positive to negative

claims.claim: CatBoost with native categorical handling outperformed XGBoost and Random Forest (both with SMOTE) on the same feature set: ROC-AUC 0.941 vs 0.929 vs 0.926; residual spatial autocorrelation was weak (Moran's I = 0.074, p < 0.001).
claims.quote: ROC-AUC: 0.941496 (highest among all models) ... XGBoost ROC-AUC: 0.929375 ... RF ROC-AUC: 0.926009 ... Moran's I ... I = 0.073620 (p < 0.001), indicating "relatively weak positive spatial autocorrelation."

claims.claim: Measurement error in traffic volume (the most common exposure predictor in safety performance functions) attenuates the estimated effect of that predictor toward zero and inflates overdispersion — i.e. a noisy AADT proxy will yield a biased-low exposure coefficient and more apparent unexplained variance.
claims.quote: One of the most common and important predictors in safety performance functions (SPFs) is traffic volume which is known to be measured with uncertainty. Such measurement errors can attenuate the respective predictors' effect and also increase dispersion.

claims.claim: A negative binomial SPF that explicitly models measurement error in traffic volume (MENB, using a measurement-error model built from traffic-flow time-series data) outperforms the standard negative binomial SPF in Monte Carlo simulation when measurement errors are large.
claims.quote: The proposed approach (denoted by MENB) was compared with the traditional negative binomial (NB) technique by way of Monte Carlo simulation... The simulation results showed that MENB outperformed NB when large measurement errors are present.

claims.claim: When traffic volume is measured with error, the conventional NB SPF systematically underestimates predicted accident counts for high-volume, long road segments and overestimates them for low-volume, short segments — the bias is not uniform but depends on exposure magnitude.
claims.quote: Additionally, in the presence of measurement errors, the NB has underestimated the predicted number of accidents for heavy traffic on long road segments and vice versa.

claims.claim: The method was estimated with full Bayes MCMC and applied to two empirical datasets of 131 and 130 road segments in British Columbia, Canada (segment-level, not area/cell-level).
claims.quote: Both approaches were applied to two datasets corresponding to 131 and 130 road segments in British Columbia. The full Bayes method was utilized for parameter estimation, performance evaluation and inference through the use of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques.

claims.claim: In a 250x250m grid model of Barcelona accidents, exposure/activity proxies (traffic variation and mobile-phone footfall) were the strongest SHAP drivers, ahead of infrastructure features (traffic lights/signs), POI density and road-type index.
claims.quote: Traffic variation...Human mobility has a big impact on accidents as well...Number of traffic lights and horizontal signs...Areas with more business premises...Road Type Index.

claims.claim: Road class and speed limit were encoded per cell as length-weighted indices (road type × length, speed limit × length in each cell) rather than raw counts, and intersections as a composite of count plus mean distance to the 3 nearest intersections.
claims.quote: TomTom provides all the roads in the city classified by type. We created an index based on the type of roads and their length in every cell. [...] We created an index based on the number of road intersections in a cell and the average distance to the three closest road intersections.

claims.claim: The standard deviation of hourly traffic within a cell was used as a proxy for peak/variable traffic exposure and emerged as the top feature.
claims.quote: We used the standard deviation of hourly traffic in all roads within a cell as a proxy to identify areas with high peaks and variations of traffic.

claims.claim: A Regression Kriging model with a Random Forest regressor on 250x250m cells achieved R2 = 0.71 for accident prediction.
claims.quote: We trained a Regression Kriging model using a Random Forest regressor for the regression part. [...] We obtained an R2 score of 0.71.

claims.claim: The feature set combined open data (OSM building footprints and road intersections, municipal accident and signaling data) with premium data (TomTom traffic, POI by trade division, Vodafone footfall, working population), so the strongest exposure proxies here were NOT derived from open data alone.
claims.quote: We selected Vodafone 250x250m cell grid as our base support and aggregated our data and performed our analyses with this support.

claims.claim: In a leave-one-out ablation on OSM-derived road graphs (DE, MA, MD, NV), removing graph-structural features (node in/out-degree and betweenness centrality) lowers accident-classification AUROC by about 6.9% on average, a larger drop than removing weather (2.3%) or measured AADT traffic volume (1.2%); e.g. NV falls from 91.62 to 82.56 AUROC and MD from 87.51 to 79.77 without structural features.
claims.quote: Removing graph-structural features reduces the performance by 6.9%. On the other hand, removing weather and traffic volume reduces performance by 2.3% and 1.2%, respectively. See Table 3 for the results, which justifies graph-structural features are the most significant features.

claims.claim: OSM road category (24 binary tags: oneway, motorway, trunk, primary, secondary, tertiary, residential, living street, link roads, unclassified, etc.) plus road length is the second most important feature group: dropping 'road information' cuts AUROC from 87.61 to 82.99 (DE), 87.51 to 80.63 (MD) and 91.62 to 84.24 (NV), while dropping official AADT changes AUROC by at most ~1.3 points.

Official AADT is available for only ~1.3-3.1% of OSM road segments in the states where it exists at all (DE 3.14%, MA 1.34%, MD 1.76%, NV 1.38%; none for IA, IL, MN, MT), which is why the authors treat volume as an auxiliary transfer-learning target rather than a primary input; using AADT prediction as an auxiliary task gives a relative gain of 1.1% AUROC and 7.9% MAE over single-task learning.
claims.quote: Lastly, we find that combining traffic volume and accident prediction yields a relative improvement of 7.9% in MAE and 1.1% in AUROC over STL, averaged over the four states with traffic volume records. [...] In our dataset, we notice that the percentage of roads where volume reports are available is pretty low (cf. Table 1).

claims.claim: Recommended encodings in the benchmark: node in-degree and out-degree as one-hot vectors (dimension = graph max degree, ~6-8), betweenness centrality as a real-valued fraction of shortest paths, road length in meters as a raw real value, road category as a 24-dim multi-hot vector, and AADT as a yearly real-valued average vehicle count; no log transform or density normalisation is applied.
claims.quote: For node degrees, we encode node degree values as one-hot vectors with a dimension of the graph's max degree. We encode two vectors for every node's in-degree and out-degree. For betweenness centrality scores, we generate a real-value feature that measures the ratio of shortest paths between all node pairs that contain a certain node. [...] We encode the physical length of the road in meters as a real-value feature. We encode the road category as a 24-dimensional characteristic vector for each edge, with each entry as either 0 or 1

claims.claim: A plain MLP on the same node features (degrees, betweenness, weather) without graph message passing achieves only 56-77 AUROC per state, whereas GraphSAGE over the OSM graph reaches 82-92 AUROC (average ~87%), with positive rates of only 0.05-0.23% of edges per month; Node2Vec/DeepWalk embeddings alone already lift MLP to ~70-92 AUROC, showing neighbourhood/structural context is the dominant signal.

A quantile regression forest trained on ~99k road segments with empirical AADT from 46 countries, using only open/global predictors (road class, population density at several scales, GDP/HDI, travel-time-weighted betweenness centrality), reaches pseudo-R2 ≈ 0.74 on a 20% hold-out set, i.e. open-data proxies explain roughly three quarters of the variance in log-AADT on extra-urban roads.
claims.quote: pseudo-R2 were very similar: 0.7418 and 0.7407, respectively ... 92.1% (18 301 out of 19 863 observations in the validation set) of the observed AADT values fell within the 90% prediction intervals

claims.claim: Road type (highway/primary/secondary) is by far the strongest single predictor of traffic volume, with GDP per capita, large-radius betweenness centrality (eBetw240) and population within a 2 km circle around the segment the next most important variables.
claims.quote: Road type (GP_RTP) was clearly the most important explanatory variable in the QRF model, followed by the variables eMeanGDP, eBetw240 and eMeanCirclePop

claims.claim: Betweenness centrality of the road graph, weighted by travel time and computed at two cutoff scales (60 and 240 minutes), is a useful exposure proxy because it separates short-distance and long-distance through-trips on a segment.
claims.quote: Edge and node betweenness centrality using travel time as weights, measuring "number of long distance trips" and "short distance trips passing through an edge" ... eBetw60, eBetw240

claims.claim: AADT should be modelled on a natural-log scale because the empirical distribution is strongly right-skewed; population-type predictors are built as multi-scale aggregates (local 2 km radius vs. larger neighbourhoods) rather than a single density value.
claims.quote: Due to the right-skewed distribution of the empirical AADT values...we transformed AADT with the natural logarithm before fitting the QRF models.

claims.claim: Empirical traffic counts cover only ~3% of the extra-urban road network even in a 46-country compilation, which is why model-based AADT proxies are needed; the resulting global dataset exists for 1975, 1990, 2000 and 2015 but historical layers are less reliable.
claims.quote: 99 328 edges with empirical AADT values assigned to them, which corresponds to 3.0% of the edges in the entire road network ... assess the reliability of the reconstructed historical road networks for their area of interest, particularly for the years 1975 and 1990

claims.claim: Across contiguous US counties, OSM road length is almost always lower than Census TIGER road length: the completeness ratio R_t = L_OSM / L_TIGER is below 1 in nearly all counties, with only seven counties exceeding 1 — so OSM-derived road-density / network features systematically undercount roads relative to the official baseline.
claims.quote: Most of the R_t values are below 1, and only seven counties in the contiguous United States have an R_t value larger than 1.

claims.claim: OSM road data completeness and positional accuracy are significantly better in metropolitan counties than in nonmetropolitan and rural counties (ANOVA on mean R_t: F = 74.28, p < 0.05), implying OSM-based exposure proxies carry an urban/rural bias that confounds comparisons between dense and sparse zones.
claims.quote: The results show that the OSM road data in metropolitan counties have better completeness and positional accuracy than those in nonmetropolitan and rural counties. ... ANOVA analysis shows that there are significant differences in the average R_t values among metro, nonmetro, and rural counties (F-statistic = 74.28, p < 0.05).

claims.claim: OSM road-data quality is spatially clustered rather than randomly distributed across counties (global Moran's I = 0.558, p < 0.001), with low-low clusters concentrated in the western US — so OSM measurement error in area-level models is spatially autocorrelated and can be absorbed into regional/spatial effects.
claims.quote: This dataset produced a Moran's I value of 0.558 (p < 0.001) ... most of the low-low clusters are in the western United States

claims.claim: Positional accuracy of OSM roads was measured as the share of OSM road length falling within 1–5 m buffers of TIGER roads (individual-buffer ratio R_i and dissolved-buffer ratio R_d), and metro/nonmetro/rural differences were statistically significant (p < 0.05) at every buffer distance — relevant when snapping crashes or POIs to OSM segments or computing cell-level road length.
claims.quote: we derived dissolved buffers for the TIGER roads...and also derived the dissolved roads for the OSM roads ... from 1 to 5 m ... The boxplots show that the OSM road data in metro counties have better positional accuracy than the OSM road data in nonmetro and rural counties.

claims.claim: The authors state that inconsistent OSM road completeness can materially change the output of downstream applications that take the road network as input, which is a caveat for using OSM graph metrics (centrality, density) as exposure proxies in crash models.
claims.quote: the quality of road data can significantly impact the results if road data are used as the input in different applications ... poor completeness of OSM road data may reduce the number of egresses in wildfire evacuation simulation, which can significantly impact the derived ETEs.

claims.claim: At the TAZ (traffic analysis zone) level, a spatially-weighted XGBoost (Geo-XGBoost) that encodes geographic proximity of neighboring zones outperforms non-spatial tree ensembles (Random Forest, GradientBoostingRegressor, LightGBM, XGBoost) for crash-count prediction, with RMSE reduced by 1.17%-23.14%, MAE by 0.42%-24.74%, and R2 improved by 2.42%-45.03%.
claims.quote: Results show that Geo-XGBoost outperforms traditional models, including Random Forest, GradientBoostingRegressor, LightGBM, and XGBoost, achieving a reduction in RMSE of 1.17% to 23.14%, a decrease in MAE of 0.42% to 24.74%, and an improvement in R^2 of 2.42% to 45.03%.

claims.claim: Zone-level road network pattern features (grid-like suburban layouts and high-accessibility road networks) are among the strongest correlates of crash risk, i.e. network-structure/accessibility proxies carry real predictive signal in area-level crash models.
claims.quote: The analysis further identifies critical road network patterns, such as suburban grids and high-accessibility road networks, that exhibit a higher correlation with crash risk, offering valuable insights for targeted traffic safety interventions.

claims.claim: The model combines static road-network-pattern features with dynamic traffic-flow (exposure) features at the TAZ level and uses interpretable ML (post-hoc explanation) to recover feature-crash relationships, rather than relying only on network structure.
claims.quote: Interpretable machine learning techniques are employed to uncover the relationships between road network patterns, dynamic traffic flow, and crash risk.

claims.claim: Area-level crash models that assume spatial homogeneity and uniform neighbor influence underperform; explicitly modeling nonlinear spatial dependence and local variation (spatial weighting of neighbors) is needed when using zonal network/exposure proxies.
claims.quote: Traditional crash risk prediction models often assume spatial homogeneity and uniform influence from neighboring areas, neglecting nonlinear spatial dependencies and regional variations. ... The authors propose a geography extreme gradient boosting (Geo-XGBoost) model incorporating spatial weighting to account for geographic proximity and local variations.

claims.claim: A trivial baseline using only the OSM road class (highway tag), 'class_only', is the best or near-best uncalibrated predictor of car counts in several cities: Spearman rho = 0.779 (Oxford), 0.673 (Melbourne), 0.706 (Toronto), 0.593 (Leeds), 0.544 (Zurich), beating OD-based centrality/assignment tools (cityseer, AequilibraE) in Oxford and Melbourne.
claims.quote: oxford-v1,car,uncalibrated,baseline,class_only,T1_open_covariates,292,0.779,0.688,1.0 ... melbourne-v1,car,uncalibrated,baseline,class_only,T1_open_covariates,2120,0.673,0.46,1.0 ... toronto-v1,car,uncalibrated,baseline,class_only,T1_open_covariates,11317,0.706,0.534,1.0

claims.claim: For heavy-vehicle flows, the OSM road-class-only baseline wins in every case with heavy counts (Leeds rho 0.571, Melbourne 0.574, Oxford 0.619, Toronto 0.68), ahead of betweenness/OD-based tools.
claims.quote: leeds-v1,heavy,uncalibrated,baseline,class_only,T1_open_covariates,415,0.571,0.535,1.0 ... toronto-v1,heavy,uncalibrated,baseline,class_only,T1_open_covariates,9076,0.68,0.627,1.0

claims.claim: For pedestrian flows, a simple OSM POI 'attractor_density' baseline (rho 0.589 Oxford, 0.622 Melbourne, 0.548 Toronto) massively outperforms network-centrality / OD-flow tools, which score near zero or negative for walking (cityseer -0.009 Oxford, 0.02 Toronto; AequilibraE -0.062 Oxford, -0.142 Toronto).
claims.quote: oxford-v1,walking,uncalibrated,baseline,attractor_density,T1_open_covariates,124,0.589,0.404,0.992 / oxford-v1,walking,uncalibrated,cityseer_od,dispersed,T2_synthetic_od,124,-0.009,-5.816,0.645 / toronto-v1,walking,uncalibrated,aequilibrae,aon,T2_synthetic_od,11310,-0.142,-6.673,0.495

claims.claim: For cycling, distance to city centre ('centre_distance') is the best single open covariate in Oxford (rho 0.658), Toronto (0.559), Zurich (0.278) and Leuven (0.259), beating OD-based centrality in each; cycling is predicted worse than car overall (max rho 0.66 vs 0.78).
claims.quote: oxford-v1,cycling,uncalibrated,baseline,centre_distance,T1_open_covariates,240,0.658,0.338,1.0 ... toronto-v1,cycling,uncalibrated,baseline,centre_distance,T1_open_covariates,10299,0.559,0.272,1.0

claims.claim: Where OD-based centrality/assignment (AequilibraE user-equilibrium, cityseer) beats class-only for cars (Leeds rho 0.639, Toronto 0.744, Zurich 0.717), it does so only in rank order: its log-scale R2 is strongly negative (-2.1 to -7.8), so raw centrality/assigned flows are useful as rank proxies for exposure but need calibration (e.g., log transform plus regression) before being used as magnitudes; the benchmark itself scores on Spearman rho and log R2.
claims.quote: toronto-v1,car,uncalibrated,aequilibrae,ue_bfw,T2_synthetic_od,11317,0.744,-2.091,0.876 ... zurich-v1,car,uncalibrated,cityseer_od,default,T2_synthetic_od,102,0.717,-7.773,0.961 (columns: case_id,mode,track,tool,variant,input_tier,n_sites,rho,log_r2,coverage)

claims.claim: On a three-year Hillsborough County (Florida) urban network dataset, a micro-level Bayesian spatial joint model (zonal crashes = sum of expected crashes of road entities in the zone) achieved better overall fit and predictive performance than a macro-level Bayesian CAR zonal model.
claims.quote: Results revealed that the micro-level model has better overall fit and predictive performance, provides better insights about the micro factors that closely contribute to crash occurrence, and leads to more direct countermeasures.

claims.claim: Macro-level (zonal) crash models are justified mainly by lower data requirements and suitability for long-term transportation planning, not by superior predictive accuracy.
claims.quote: Whereas the macro-level crash analysis has the advantage of requirement of less detailed data, providing additional instructions for non-traffic engineering issues, as well as serving as an indispensable tool in incorporating safety considerations into long term transportation planning.

claims.claim: The paper proposes and empirically evaluates two alternative formulations of zonal crash frequency: aggregating crash statistics to a spatial scale and relating them to macroscopic factors (macro), versus summing expected crashes of all road entities inside the zone (micro).
claims.quote: Typically, zonal safety level is evaluated by relating aggregated crash statistics at a certain spatial scale to various macroscopic factors. Another potential solution is from the micro level perspective, in which zonal crash frequency is estimated by summing up the expected crashes of all the road entities located within the zones of interest.

claims.claim: An integrated hot-zone screening approach that combines separate macro-level and micro-level screening results was proposed to exploit the merits of both levels.
claims.quote: An integrated hot zone identification approach was then proposed to exploit the merits of separate macro and micro screening results. The research was based on a three-year dataset of an urban road network in Hillsborough County, Florida, U.S.

claims.claim: In a random-parameter negative binomial crash-frequency model for Greater Melbourne, zone-level built-environment proxies — employment density, road density, highway (major road) density, job-housing balance, land-use mixture, and bus route density — are statistically significant predictors of crash counts, i.e. density- and share-type encodings of OSM-derivable features carry signal for area-level crash models.
claims.quote: Factors including density (e.g., employment density), network design (e.g., road density and highway density), land use diversity (e.g., job-housing balance and land use mixture), and public transit accessibility (e.g., bus route density) are significantly associated with crash occurrence.

claims.claim: Segmenting the study area into traffic-density-based zones (TDZs) rather than administrative/planning zones yields a better-fitting crash frequency model (improved goodness-of-fit), suggesting that the choice of spatial unit for aggregation materially affects area-level crash modelling.
claims.quote: Results indicate that the data segmentation based on TDZs is instrumental in establishing a more refined crash model compared to traditional planning-based zones, as demonstrated by improved goodness-of-fit measures.

claims.claim: Dynamic traffic-flow exposure variables derived from the Macroscopic Fundamental Diagram (shockwave velocity and congestion index) have heterogeneous (random-parameter) effects on crash frequency across zones, so a single fixed coefficient for congestion/flow exposure is inadequate.
claims.quote: Furthermore, the unobserved heterogeneity effects of the shockwave velocity and congestion index on crashes are revealed. The study highlights the significance of incorporating dynamic traffic flow variables in understanding crash frequency variations across different spatial units.

claims.claim: The association between zone-level covariates and crash frequency was estimated with a random parameter negative binomial regression, the standard count model family for macro-level crash prediction with overdispersion.
claims.quote: The association between the potential influencing factors and crash frequency is examined using a random parameter negative binomial regression model.
